summary.text: The defining sum satisfies \(a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\); Fermat’s theorem and \(\binom{k+2(p-1)}2-\binom{k}2\in(p-1)\mathbb Z\) make both coefficients invariant modulo an odd prime, so the result follows inductively. The base value modulo an odd prime is obtained because every nonfinal summand contains \(2^{2(p-1)}-1\), while the final exponent is a multiple of \(p-1\); for \(p=2\), the recurrence shows all positive-index terms are odd.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_k=\frac{k(k+1)}2=\binom{k+1}{2}
\]
be the \(k\)-th triangular number. With the convention that an empty product is \(1\), the sequence is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_k}\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

We begin by deriving a recurrence for \(a(n)\). In the sum defining \(a(n+1)\), the term with \(k=n\) is
\[
2^{T_n}\prod_{j=n+1}^{n}(2^j-1)=2^{T_n}.
\]
For every earlier term, with \(0\leq k<n\), the product ending at \(n\) can be split as
\[
\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}(2^j-1)
=(2^n-1)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
Thus the common factor \(2^n-1\) can be taken out of all the earlier terms, giving
\[
\boxed{\ a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}.\ }
\tag{1}
\]
Also, directly from the defining sum,
\[
a(1)=2^{T_0}=1.
\tag{2}
\]

We first dispose of the prime \(p=2\). We claim that
\[
a(n)\equiv 1\pmod 2
\qquad(n\geq 1).
\tag{3}
\]
This follows by induction. It is true for \(n=1\) by (2). Suppose it is true for some \(n\geq1\). Then \(2^n-1\) is odd. Moreover,
\[
T_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2\geq1,
\]
so \(2^{T_n}\) is even. Applying (1), an odd number times the odd number \(a(n)\), plus an even number, is odd. Hence \(a(n+1)\) is odd, proving (3). Consequently both \(a(n)\) and \(a(n+2)\) are congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2\). Since \(2(p-1)=2\) when \(p=2\), the desired result follows in this case.

It remains to treat an odd prime \(p\). Put
\[
d=p-1,\qquad L=2(p-1)=2d.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(2\not\equiv0\pmod p\), and Fermat's theorem gives
\[
2^{p-1}=2^d\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{4}
\]
It follows in particular that
\[
2^{dq}\equiv1\pmod p
\tag{5}
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(q\).

We record two periodicity consequences of (4). First,
\[
2^{n+L}=2^{n+2d}=2^n(2^d)^2\equiv2^n\pmod p.
\tag{6}
\]
Second, triangular exponents have the needed periodicity. For arbitrary nonnegative integers \(x,d\), direct expansion gives
\[
\binom{x+2d}{2}
= inom{x}{2}+d(2x+2d-1).
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, multiplying by \(2\), the difference between the two sides reduces to the identity
\[
(x+2d)(x+2d-1)-x(x-1)=2d(2x+2d-1).
\]
Taking \(d=p-1\), the extra exponent on the right side of (7) is a multiple of \(p-1\). Therefore (5) yields
\[
2^{\binom{x+L}{2}}\equiv2^{\binom{x}{2}}\pmod p.
\tag{8}
\]
In terms of triangular numbers, taking \(x=n+1\) says
\[
2^{T_{n+L}}=2^{\binom{n+L+1}{2}}
\equiv 2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}=2^{T_n}\pmod p.
\tag{9}
\]
Thus both parts on the right side of recurrence (1)—the coefficient \(2^n-1\) and the inhomogeneous term \(2^{T_n}\)—repeat modulo \(p\) when \(n\) is increased by \(L\).

To start an induction using the recurrence, we now prove the initial congruence
\[
a(1+L)\equiv a(1)\pmod p.
\tag{10}
\]
Since
\[
1+L=1+2(p-1)=2p-1,
\]
consider the defining sum for \(a(2p-1)\). Its index \(k\) runs from \(0\) through \(2p-2=L\).

If \(k<L\), then the product
\[
\prod_{j=k+1}^{L}(2^j-1)
\]
contains the factor corresponding to \(j=L\), namely
\[
2^L-1=2^{2(p-1)}-1.
\]
By (4),
\[
2^{2(p-1)}=(2^{p-1})^2\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so this factor is \(0\) modulo \(p\). Hence every summand with \(k<L\) vanishes modulo \(p\).

Only the last summand, for \(k=L=2p-2\), remains. Its product is empty, so it equals
\[
2^{T_L}=2^{\binom{L+1}{2}}=2^{\binom{2p-1}{2}}.
\]
The exponent is
\[
\binom{2p-1}{2}
=\frac{(2p-1)(2p-2)}2
=(2p-1)(p-1),
\]
a multiple of \(p-1\). By (5), this last summand is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(p\). We have therefore shown
\[
a(2p-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Together with \(a(1)=1\), this proves (10).

We can now finish by induction on \(n\geq1\). The base case \(n=1\) is (10). Assume for some \(n\geq1\) that
\[
a(n+L)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\tag{11}
\]
Apply recurrence (1) at the indices \(n+L\) and \(n\):
\[
a(n+L+1)=(2^{n+L}-1)a(n+L)+2^{T_{n+L}},
\]
while
\[
a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}.
\]
By (6),
\[
2^{n+L}-1\equiv2^n-1\pmod p;
\]
by the induction hypothesis (11),
\[
a(n+L)\equiv a(n)\pmod p;
\]
and by (9),
\[
2^{T_{n+L}}\equiv2^{T_n}\pmod p.
\]
Substitution in the first recurrence therefore gives
\[
a(n+L+1)
\equiv(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{T_n}
=a(n+1)\pmod p.
\]
This is exactly the induction statement for \(n+1\).

Thus, for every odd prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
The parity argument established the same conclusion for \(p=2\), so the result holds for every prime \(p\).
